## Agentic Canvas: Design With AI Agents9 min read

Reading Time:   6 minutes

AI agents can generate a website in minutes. Then you want to move a button, compare two layouts, collect a few screenshots, or fix the spacing yourself. Suddenly you are back to explaining a visual change in another prompt. Sometimes it is easier to drag than to prompt.

That is why we built Agentic Canvas by AgentGrid.io. It is a free AI design canvas where you and an MCP-capable agent work on the same real HTML and CSS page. Bring in HTML, start with a design or image, or ask your agent to build a page. Then select, move, resize and edit what it made. You can open Agentic Canvas without creating an account. [...] Canvas export options and an illustrative AgentGrid.io sharing dialog

Export a file or choose to host and share it on AgentGrid.io.

## What stays local, and what requires an account?

You can start designing in your browser for free, without signing up. Your files live in that browser on that device, not in an automatic cross-device backup. Export a copy of work you want to keep outside the browser. Connecting an external agent lets it read the canvas and uses a network connection, so local does not mean offline. Sharing or publishing through AgentGrid.io is optional and requires an account.

Illustration of local canvas files on a laptop with a free label

Local files stay in this browser on this device until you choose to share. Export a backup of work you want to keep. [...] Think of it as a place where the person who sees what needs fixing and the agent that can write the code work on the same thing.

Agentic Canvas visual design interface with a live Kestrel Labs web page and inspector

Design visually: edit a live page with layers and layout controls.

## Why we needed a canvas for AI agents

### 1. Visual collaboration without another prompt loop

When you make a landing page, product screen or marketing asset with Claude or ChatGPT, the first draft is only the start. You may want three copies of a hero, a tighter grid or a different call to action. Describing every visual decision in chat is slow, especially when you already know exactly what to change.

New Project! 🖼️ Run your AI agents on an infinite canvasTry it now

# Michael Yagudaev

# AgentGrid — An Infinite Canvas for AI Agents

September 10, 2026∙2 min read

AgentGrid cover

I didn't believe a Figma-like canvas for AI agents would work. Then I used it every day for a month and couldn't go back.

## How it started

My friend Souren built the first version of AgentGrid to scale his own development on an AI trading platform. He showed it to me early. I was skeptical — a big infinite canvas where you run agents on panes? Sounded like a gimmick. I'd seen plenty of "visual node" tools that looked impressive in a demo and fell apart under real work.

About a month later he convinced me to give it a serious try.

## The unlock

Two things won me over. [...] ## The unlock

Two things won me over.

Persistent sessions. AgentGrid saves sessions to disk, and everything around a session — images, notes, research pages, browser pages — lives on the same canvas together. You don't lose context when you close your laptop. You come back to the exact board with the exact agents mid-thought. That sounds small until you've lived without it.

Switching between projects. I work on a lot of things. With a terminal-only workflow, juggling three agents across three repos meant three tmux sessions, three directories, no shared context. On a canvas it's just… there. Drag a pane, spawn another, keep going.

I 3x'd my productivity within the first 30 days. (I also broke AgentGrid a few times — early-adopter tax. Souren was very patient.) [...] The real tell: when AgentGrid was down during development for up to ~12 hours a day, going back to the old terminal-only workflow was miserable. I hated it. That's when I knew we had something.

So I started working on it full-time with Souren. We kept wanting more features, and we kept wanting to make it a great product.

## What it is now

AgentGrid — an infinite canvas for AI coding agents. Run agents, pin notes, open browsers, drop in research — all on one persistent board.

results.title: How agents connect — AgentGrid docs
results.content:
## Agentic Canvas is a separate connection

An agent added to Agentic Canvas acts on the human's open canvas tab only. That connection does not reach AgentGrid.io workspaces or artifacts, and an AgentGrid.io connection does not reach local canvas files. See Connect your agent to the canvas.

## Questions and answers

How is the route chosen? Browser-tab assistants use an official connector or plug-in. Desktop and server agents self-connect. Unattended agents use advance consent through an invite.

What must a human decide? The agent name, workspace access, and `read`, `write`, `share`, or `publish` capabilities.

What proves connection is complete? The agent has a named identity, can list the intended reachable workspace, and creates directly there without a claim step. [...] ## After it connects

 It lists its reachable workspaces—the workspaces it has permission to access—and creates directly in the one selected for the task. Nothing to accept, nothing to claim.
 Its changes appear in every artifact's history, under its own name.
 It stays within the capabilities you granted, checked on every request. Those capabilities are fixed: to change them, remove the agent and invite it again.
 It appears in Agent administration, where you can remove it. Workspace grants are managed in Workspace access. See Revoke an agent.

## Agents on Agentic Canvas

Adding an agent to Agentic Canvas is separate from connecting it to AgentGrid.io. It lets the agent work on your canvas files only. See Connect your agent to the canvas.
